narrative.text: Front cover displaying the publication title, Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products.
Blank inside front cover page with no extracted text.
Half-title page displaying the publication title, Digital transformation handbook for reporting substandard and falsified medical products.

Copyright and publication page providing ISBNs (978-92-4-012074-7 electronic, 978-92-4-012075-4 print), CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO licensing terms, suggested 2026 WHO citation, CIP data link, third-party material reuse policies, and general legal disclaimers.

First page of the table of contents (page iii), listing front matter, Introduction, Chapter 1 (Assess the current state and enabling environment), Chapter 2 (Establish a shared understanding and governance framework), Chapter 3 (Define the future state), and Chapter 4 (Determine the requirements).

Conclusion of the table of contents (page iv), listing Chapter 5 (Plan the implementation), Chapter 6 (Monitor, evaluate and scale), Chapter 7 (Share implementation experiences), References, Resources, and Annexes 1 through 7.

Acknowledgements (page v) crediting lead authors from WHO and United Health Futures (UHF), technical reviewers and independent experts, national regulatory authority contributors from Chile (ISP) and South Africa (SAHPRA), public consultation participants, declarations of interest, and funding from the Gates Foundation and the UK Fleming Fund.
List of abbreviations and acronyms (page vi), defining terms from BPMN, DIIG, FHIR, and GSMS through NMRA, PMS, RACI, Rb-PMS, SaaS, SMART, UAT, UHF, and WHO.

First page of the glossary (page vii), defining terms from active pharmacovigilance, adverse drug reactions, business process, data element, digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation through enabling environment, end user, enterprise architecture, evaluation, falsified medical products, features, and functional requirements.

Second page of the glossary (page viii), defining generic product, health care professional, interoperability, Member State Mechanism (MSM), monitoring, non-functional requirements, open source, open standards, organogram, passive pharmacovigilance, persona, pharmacovigilance, polypharmacy, post-market surveillance (PMS), and registry.
Conclusion of the glossary (page ix), defining SMART Guidelines, substandard products, trade item, unregistered medical products, user acceptance testing (UAT), and workflow.
Blank separator page preceding the Introduction with no extracted text.

Opening of the Introduction (page 1), explaining the health, antimicrobial resistance, and socioeconomic threats posed by substandard and falsified medical products, stating WHO definitions, describing risk-based post-market surveillance (Rb-PMS), and introducing national regulatory authority (NMRA) and WHO Global Surveillance and Monitoring System (GSMS) reporting by frontline health care professionals.

Continuation of the Introduction (page 2), contrasting paper-based reporting limitations with standards-based digital reporting applications piloted in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania, and presenting the first half of Table 1 on the intended audience and purpose for Chapters 1 through 4.

Conclusion of Table 1 for Chapters 5 through 7 and guidance on how and when to use the handbook (page 3), including scenarios for transitioning from paper or isolated tools to interoperable digital reporting systems and prerequisite alignment with national digital health strategies and the WHO DIIG framework.

Figure 1 (page 4), illustrating the seven phases, key steps, and reference toolkits for planning and implementing a digital health enterprise adapted from the WHO Digital Implementation Investment Guide (DIIG).

Overview of the WHO SMART Guidelines five-layer pathway (L1 Narrative through L5 Dynamic) and Figure 2 (page 5), explaining how this handbook provides L1 and L2 guidance for localizing and implementing digital solutions for reporting substandard and falsified medical products.

Explanation of how the handbook was developed (page 6), drawing on global health care professional and NMRA consultations, benchmarking, real-world pilot implementations in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania, Principles for Digital Development, the WHO DIIG, and the WHO/ITU National eHealth Strategy Toolkit.
Section divider page for Chapter 1: Assess the current state and enabling environment.

Opening of Chapter 1 (page 8), listing inputs, outputs, and resources for assessing the current state and enabling environment, followed by Section 1.1 on analysing key stakeholders with a RACI matrix and the start of Section 1.2 on assessing country digital readiness.

Table 2 (page 9), providing sample stakeholder analysis questions across six dimensions: roles and responsibilities, information flows and interactions, influence and power, interests and expectations, engagement and collaboration, and capacity and resources.

Completion of Section 1.2 on digital readiness assessment dimensions (strategy, policy, governance, human resources, technology infrastructure, and security and privacy) and start of Section 1.3 on assessing current substandard and falsified reporting practices, pharmacovigilance synergies, data collection forms, and existing digital tools (page 10).

Table 3 (page 11), providing metrics and guiding questions for assessing technology infrastructure across network coverage, connectivity, electricity, hardware and software availability, computing infrastructure, cybersecurity, privacy, and data ownership.

Continuation of Section 1.3 on evaluating information flows, categorizing digital solutions, and identifying reporting barriers, accompanied by Table 4 with guiding questions for assessing pharmacovigilance and substandard and falsified medicines data collection forms and data usage (page 12).

Table 5 (page 13), mapping common challenges and barriers to substandard and falsified product reporting across capacity, regulatory support, health system practices, economic, social, education, and technology categories to potential design solutions (including a note on anonymous reporting trade-offs), followed by the Chapter 1 checklist.
Section divider page for Chapter 2: Establish a shared understanding and governance framework.

Opening of Chapter 2 (page 15), listing inputs, outputs, and resources for establishing a shared understanding and governance framework, and presenting Section 2.1 on reviewing regulatory policies for pharmacovigilance and quality surveillance integration, reporting obligations, and enforcement mechanisms.

Sections 2.2, 2.3, and 2.4 (page 16), detailing multisectoral policy alignment (law enforcement, customs, procurement, ICT ministries, and regional/global regulators), governance and leadership structures (national steering committee, technical working group, advisory council, project champion, and coordinator), and SMART strategic goals.
Section 2.5 on analysing and mitigating technical, financial, and political/stakeholder risks (referencing Annex 7) and the end-of-chapter checklist for Chapter 2 (page 17).
Section divider page for Chapter 3: Define the future state.

Opening of Chapter 3 (page 19), listing inputs, outputs, and resources for defining the future state, and presenting Section 3.1 on developing a structured digital investment roadmap across short-term (1–2 years), medium-term (3–5 years), and long-term (5+ years) horizons.

Table 6 (page 20), mapping system attributes across core functionality and user experience, data management and analysis, collaboration and communication, regulatory compliance and governance, and scalability and maintainability to short-, medium-, and long-term implementation priorities.

Section 3.2 (page 21) on linking the substandard and falsified reporting application as a point-of-service application within a DIIG-aligned digital health enterprise architecture, highlighting open standards and interoperability (TOGAF, HL7 FHIR), cybersecurity and data protection, and the Chapter 3 checklist.

Figure 3 (page 22), presenting the WHO DIIG digital health enterprise architecture framework across point-of-service applications, the interoperability layer, shared business domain/registry/terminology services, data services, institution- and population-based data sources, and external systems.
Section divider page for Chapter 4: Determine the requirements.

Opening of Chapter 4 (page 24), listing inputs, outputs (user personas, scenarios, as-is/to-be business processes, data dictionary, decision logic, functional and non-functional requirements, and indicators), and resources for determining system requirements.

Sections 4.1 and 4.2 (page 25) on identifying skilled health care professional user personas and defining practical user scenarios, together with the first part of Table 7 describing the Doctor (ISCO 2211/2212) and Nurse (ISCO 2221) personas.

Continuation of Table 7 for the Pharmacist persona (ISCO 2262) and Table 8 (page 26) describing related user personas including the Individual/patient, Community health worker (ISCO 3253/3259), and Laboratory technician (ISCO 3212).

First half of Table 9 (page 27), detailing end-to-end user scenarios (discovery, initial action, accessing the reporting app, completing the report, submitting the report, and follow-up/feedback) for a Pharmacist, Doctor (general practitioner), Nurse, and Dentist.
Second half of Table 9 (page 28), detailing end-to-end reporting scenarios for a Midwife, Laboratory technician, Public health worker, Pharmacy technician, and Paramedic.

Section 4.3 (page 29) on developing as-is and to-be business processes and BPMN 2.0 workflows, accompanied by Table 10 illustrating a business process matrix entry (SF-REP-001) for suspect product detection and digital reporting by a pharmacist.

Figure 4 depicting an example workflow for reporting suspected substandard or falsified medical products to an NMRA, followed by Section 4.4 on outlining standardized data dictionaries (ICD-11, SNOMED-GPS, HL7 FHIR) and Section 4.5 on gathering functional and non-functional requirements (page 30).

Table 11 listing sample data elements (SFR.A1.DE1 through DE10: region, report type, product ID, description, product type, batch number, expiry date, substandard/falsified classification, adverse reaction/lack of efficacy flag, and issue description) and Table 12 listing sample functional requirements (SFR.FXNREQ.001–002 and product reporting user stories) (page 31).

First page of Table 13 (page 32), specifying sample non-functional requirements for security confidentiality (password protection, PHI privacy, end-to-end and at-rest encryption, secure destruction, removable media), authentication (password policies, lockout, RBAC, MFA, SAML/OpenID Connect SSO), immutable audit trails and logs, and user management.

Second page of Table 13 (page 33), continuing sample non-functional requirements across user role management, general security (vulnerability scans, penetration testing, vendor risk mitigation, UN data privacy compliance), and general system requirements (versioning, offline/online sync, backups, unstructured image storage, master data, ISO 27000, IP ownership, open-source licensing, and report import/export).

Third page of Table 13 (page 34), covering general system requirements for documentation, testing, training, and support contracts, scalability requirements, usability requirements (low-literacy design, validation, multilingual support, responsive mobile/web UI, localization, image/barcode capture, auto-save, low-bandwidth performance), and central configuration.

Conclusion of Table 13 (page 35) covering system configuration (CQL + FHIR business rules, separate dev/UAT/prod environments), interoperability (mediators, APIs, FHIR back end, paper/GPS input), intermittent connectivity synchronization, and vendor delivery requirements (ITIL change management, OWASP secure coding, disaster recovery, UAT milestone acceptance), followed by the Chapter 4 checklist.
Section divider page for Chapter 5: Plan the implementation.

Opening of Chapter 5 (page 37), listing inputs, outputs, and resources for planning the implementation, introducing technology options (open source, packaged applications, SaaS), and presenting Table 14 on the steps to develop the implementation plan, develop the budget (cost drivers, TCO, budget matrix, funding), and execute implementation.

Guidance on evaluating cloud and on-premises deployment options and open-source total cost of ownership, Table 15 comparing five software options (packaged off-the-shelf, SaaS, enhancing an existing application, building from scratch, and open-source solutions), and the Chapter 5 checklist (page 38).
Section divider page for Chapter 6: Monitor, evaluate and scale.

Opening of Chapter 6 (page 40), listing inputs, outputs, and resources for monitoring, evaluation, and scaling, and presenting Section 6.1 on distinguishing intrinsic monitoring from extrinsic evaluation across the maturity life cycle of the substandard and falsified reporting application.

Figure 5 on intervention maturity over time (from prototype to national implementation) and Figure 6 (page 41) mapping monitoring goals, evaluation stages, user scale (10–100 up to 100 000+), and illustrative measurement targets across six maturity stages.

Table 16 (page 42), providing sample evaluation questions across the reporting application's life cycle for usability, efficacy in controlled/pilot settings, effectiveness in non-research settings, and cost-effectiveness.

Table 17 (page 43), outlining the six steps for developing a comprehensive monitoring and evaluation (M&E) plan: establishing the underlying framework, identifying evidence needs and objectives, designing methodologies, assigning responsibilities, scheduling timelines and resources, and summarizing the M&E implementation plan.

Table 18 (page 44), listing reference M&E measures across quality, fidelity, stability, functionality, and investment categories together with when each category is assessed (pre-implementation, pre-launch, during implementation, and post-launch).

Section 6.2 (page 45) on developing an operations, continuous improvement, and sustainability plan covering stakeholder ownership, infrastructure and cybersecurity resources, recurring training and knowledge management, operational budgeting, backups and redundancy, and change governance, followed by the Chapter 6 checklist.
Section divider page for Chapter 7: Share implementation experiences.

Chapter 7 case study (page 47) on piloting a smartphone application for reporting suspected substandard and falsified medical products in Indonesia and the United Republic of Tanzania, summarizing the four-step reporting flow, offline outbox and alert features, feasibility (36 reports of 27 products), successes, and areas requiring improvement.
First page of the numbered References list (page 48), covering citations 1 through 18 (accessed 23 April 2026).
Conclusion of the numbered References list (page 49), covering citations 19 through 37.
Resources list (page 50), providing bibliographic details and links for 17 WHO, ITU, UNICEF, HL7 FHIR, MEASURE Evaluation, GH Supply Chain, and TOGAF reference publications and tools.
Section divider page for the Annexes (page 51).

Annex 1 (page 52), summarizing the nine Principles for Digital Development: understand the existing ecosystem, share/reuse/improve, design with people, design for inclusion, build for sustainability, establish people-first data practices, create open and transparent practices, anticipate and mitigate harms, and use evidence to improve outcomes.

Annex 2 (page 53), providing a user persona worksheet template covering occupation, demographics, expected daily/weekly/monthly roles, behaviour patterns, working context and connectivity, routine challenges/pain points, and motivations and success metrics.

First page of Annex 3 (page 54), defining Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) symbols and usage rules for pool, swim lane, start/trigger event, start event message, end event, activity/task, and activity with subprocess.

Conclusion of Annex 3 (page 55), defining BPMN 2.0 symbols for activity with a business rule, sequence flow, message flow, exclusive gateway, parallel gateway, throw and catch link events, ad hoc subprocess, and loop activity.

Annex 4 (page 56), presenting a sample stakeholder RACI (responsible, accountable, consulted, informed) matrix template across activities such as defining project scope, gathering requirements, and designing UI/UX.

Annex 5 (page 57), presenting a matrix template for assessing current software applications (deployed vs. in progress) across health system organizational levels and supply chain/regulatory functional areas (forecasting, procurement, order and warehouse management, dispensing, analytics, pharmacovigilance, cold chain, NPC, and registration).

Annex 6 (page 58), presenting a visual fishbone analysis of barriers to reporting substandard and falsified medical products across health care professionals, NMRAs, and consumers, categorized by health care, NMRA-related, technology, economic, social, education/knowledge, and capacity barriers.

Annex 7 (page 59), presenting a risk management table template for recording risk ID, title, IF/THEN description, priority, impact, probability, status, mitigation steps, owner, and raised/reviewed/closed dates, illustrated with an example on inadequate training.
Back cover displaying the World Health Organization headquarters postal address in Geneva, Switzerland, and website (who.int).
